items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> x <- 2
> f <- function(y) {
+   x <- 10
+   x * y
+ }
> f(3)
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: Inside f, x <- 10 creates a local x that hides the global x = 2, so f(3) = 10 × 3 = 30. Trap: 6 uses the global x. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> x <- 1
> f <- function() {
+   x <<- 5
+   x + 1
+ }
> f()
> x
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: <<- assigns in the enclosing (here global) environment, so f() changes the global x to 5 (and returns 6). The last line prints x = 5. Trap: with <- instead of <<- the global x would stay 1. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)
A default argument may refer to another argument: b defaults to a * 2 = 6, so f(3) = 3 + 6 = 9. Trap: 3 ignores the default for b. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

A part of an R program is given below:
> x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
> y <- x[x > 2]
> sum(y)
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: x > 2 is the logical vector (FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE), so y = c(3, 4) and sum(y) = 7. Trap: 2 counts the selected elements instead of adding them. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> g <- function(n) {
+   s <- 0
+   for (i in 1:n) s <- s + i
+   s
+ }
> g(4)
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: The loop adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, and the last expression s is returned. Trap: 24 is 4! (a product, not a sum). (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> x <- 5
> h <- function(x) {
+   x <- x + 1
+   x
+ }
> h(x)
> x
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: R passes arguments by value: h works on its own copy of x and returns 6, but the global x is untouched. The last line prints 5. Trap: 6 is what h(x) returns, not the new value of x. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> v <- 1:4 * 1:2
> sum(v)
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: The shorter vector is recycled: 1:4 * c(1, 2, 1, 2) = c(1, 4, 3, 8), whose sum is 16. Trap: 30 multiplies the two sums, and 20 treats 1:2 as the single number 2; R multiplies element by element after recycling. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> f <- function(n) if (n <= 1) 1 else n * f(n - 1)
> f(4)
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: f calls itself on n − 1 until the base case n ≤ 1 returns 1: f(4) = 4 × f(3) = 4 × 3 × f(2) = 4 × 3 × 2 × f(1) = 24, the factorial of 4. Trap: 10 adds the numbers instead of multiplying them. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> x <- c(2, 4, 6)
> x[2] <- 10
> mean(x)
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: After x[2] <- 10 the vector is c(2, 10, 6), whose mean is 18/3 = 6. Trap: 4 is the mean before the change; 18 is the sum. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
A part of an R program is given below:
> a <- 3
> f <- function() {
+   a <- a + 2
+   g <- function() a * 2
+   g()
+ }
> f()
The output of the last line is:
items.explanation: Inside f, a <- a + 2 makes a local a = 5. g is defined inside f, so it finds that a (lexical scoping) and returns 5 × 2 = 10. Trap: 6 uses the global a = 3. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)
